events.title: Special court against the followers of Tiberius Gracchus
events.summary: The consuls Publius Popillius Laenas and Publius Rupilius, on the authority of the Senate, ran a special inquiry that condemned and executed or exiled supporters of Tiberius Gracchus. The philosopher Blossius of Cumae escaped to Aristonicus; Gaius Villius was reportedly sewn into a sack with snakes.
events.detail: The inquiry had no popular mandate, which is why Gaius Gracchus later passed his lex de capite civis and drove Popillius into exile (123). Scipio Nasica, the leader of the lynching, was sent on a face-saving embassy to Asia, where he died at Pergamon in 132. The land commission itself was left untouched: the Senate punished the man, not the law.
events.debate: Numbers executed are unknown; Plutarch's anecdotes about Villius and Diophanes may be embroidered.

events.title: First censorship held by two plebeians
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus and Quintus Pompeius were the first pair of plebeian censors. Metellus gave his famous speech urging compulsory marriage to raise the birth rate (de prole augenda), later read out by Augustus to the Senate.

events.title: Carbo's bill to allow tribunes to stand again
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Papirius Carbo, a Gracchan land commissioner, proposed that tribunes might be re-elected without limit. Scipio Aemilianus opposed it and declared Tiberius Gracchus justly killed; the bill failed, though re-election was later practised in fact.

events.title: Scipio Aemilianus defends the allies against the land commission
events.summary: Responding to complaints of Italian landholders whose possession of ager publicus was being challenged, Scipio Aemilianus had judicial power over disputed land transferred from the Gracchan commissioners to the consul Tuditanus, who promptly left for Illyricum. Scipio died suddenly days later.
events.detail: This is the first time the allied question appears as politics in its own right: the Gracchan law reclaimed public land that Latins and Italians had occupied, often for generations. The transfer effectively paralysed the commission's judicial work, though boundary stones (cippi) of the commissioners Carbo, Fulvius Flaccus and Gaius Gracchus show that assignations continued into the 120s.
events.debate: How much land the commission actually redistributed is disputed; the census jump of 131-125 (318,823 to 394,736) is read by some as evidence of large-scale settlement, by others as better registration.

events.title: Sempronius Tuditanus campaigns against the Iapydes
events.summary: The consul Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus, after an initial reverse, defeated the Iapydes and Histri at the head of the Adriatic with the help of Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus, and celebrated a triumph on 1 October 129. He set up a dedication to the river Timavus, fragments of whose verse inscription survive at Aquileia.

events.title: Gaius Gracchus quaestor in Sardinia
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus served as quaestor to the consul Lucius Aurelius Orestes in Sardinia (126-124), winning goodwill by persuading Sardinian communities to clothe the army after the Senate refused. When the Senate prolonged Orestes' command to keep Gaius away, he returned without leave and defended himself before the censors.

events.title: Fulvius Flaccus answers Massalia's appeal against the Salluvii
events.summary: The consul Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, sent to aid Rome's ally Massalia against the Salluvii (Salyes), became the first Roman commander to campaign beyond the Alps for conquest, opening the war that produced Gallia Transalpina. Gaius Sextius Calvinus continued it in 124-122, destroying the oppidum of Entremont.
events.detail: Flaccus had just failed to carry his citizenship proposal, and his removal to Gaul was convenient to the Senate. The Salluvian oppidum of Entremont, with its sculptures of seated warriors and skull niches, shows a destruction layer that excavators link to Sextius' campaign; the Roman garrison at the springs nearby became Aquae Sextiae (122).

events.title: Lex Sempronia on consular provinces
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus' law required the Senate to name the two consular provinces before the consular elections, and barred tribunes from vetoing the decision. It aimed to stop the Senate from rewarding or punishing consuls after it knew who had been elected.
events.debate: Date (123 or 122) uncertain. It remained in force until replaced by Pompey's law of 52.

events.title: Lex Sempronia militaris
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus' military law made the state supply clothing to soldiers without deducting it from their pay and forbade the enrolment of anyone under seventeen. It is a sign of the strain on the small-farmer levy that the Gracchi sought to relieve.

events.title: The Fornix Fabianus
events.summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus Allobrogicus, victor over the Allobroges and Arverni, built a triumphal arch at the east end of the Forum on the Sacra Via, the first such arch in the Forum. His grandson restored it in 57 with statues of family heroes, Aemilius Paullus and Scipio Aemilianus among them.

events.title: Assassination of Mithridates V and accession of Mithridates VI
events.summary: Mithridates V Euergetes, Rome's ally in the Aristonicus war, was murdered at Sinope, probably by courtiers, leaving his widow Laodice as regent for the boy Mithridates VI. Rome promptly took back Greater Phrygia, which Manius Aquillius had sold to Pontus. Later legend had the young king flee to the wilderness for seven years.
events.debate: Mithridates VI probably took sole power about 116-113 by imprisoning his mother and killing his brother; the immunity-to-poison tales are later legend.

events.title: Metellus campaigns against the Dalmatae
events.summary: The consul Lucius Caecilius Metellus attacked the Dalmatae, who had given no cause, wintered peacefully at Salona and celebrated a triumph as Delmaticus in 117. From the spoils he restored the Temple of Castor in the Forum.
events.detail: Appian says bluntly that Metellus wanted a triumph. The Metelli were at their peak: between 123 and 109 six members of the family held the consulship, and four celebrated triumphs.

events.title: Metellus rebuilds the Temple of Castor
events.summary: Lucius Caecilius Metellus Delmaticus rebuilt the Temple of Castor and Pollux in the Forum with Dalmatian spoils, giving it a high podium whose front became a speaker's platform used by Caesar, Clodius and others. It was rebuilt again by Tiberius in AD 6.

events.title: Marius tried for electoral bribery
events.summary: Elected praetor for 115 in last place, Gaius Marius was prosecuted for ambitus; a slave of his supporter Cassius Sabaco had been seen inside the voting enclosure. The jury divided equally and he was acquitted, a narrow escape that began his career.

events.title: Consulship of Marcus Aemilius Scaurus
events.summary: Scaurus, a patrician of impoverished family, became consul and princeps senatus, passed a sumptuary law and a law on the voting of freedmen, and triumphed over the Ligurian Gantisci and the Carni. He would dominate the Senate for a quarter of a century.

events.title: Destruction of Porcius Cato's army by the Scordisci
events.summary: The consul Gaius Porcius Cato, grandson of the Censor, was routed by the Scordisci in Thrace or Macedonia and lost his whole army. He was later convicted of extortion. The defeat opened a decade of Thracian and Celtic raids on the province of Macedonia.

battle.significance: Exposed Macedonia to raids until Minucius Rufus' victories of 109-106.

events.title: Calpurnius Bestia's peace with Jugurtha
events.summary: The consul Lucius Calpurnius Bestia, with Scaurus on his staff, invaded Numidia and then quickly accepted Jugurtha's surrender on easy terms: 30 elephants, cattle, horses and a little silver. The tribune Gaius Memmius denounced the deal as bought, leading to Jugurtha's summons to Rome.
events.debate: Sallust's whole account of senatorial venality is a moralising construct; modern scholars (e.g. Kraus, Morstein-Marx) suspect strategic caution played a part.

events.title: Silanus defeated by the Cimbri
events.summary: The consul Marcus Junius Silanus refused the Cimbri's request for land in exchange for military service and was defeated somewhere in southern Gaul, the second Roman army beaten by the migrants. He was tried and acquitted in 104.

battle.significance: Confirmed that the Cimbri could beat Roman armies in the open field.

events.title: Minucius Rufus defeats the Scordisci
events.summary: Marcus Minucius Rufus, consul 110 and proconsul of Macedonia, defeated the Scordisci and Thracian Bessi, many drowning in the frozen Hebrus. With the spoils of his triumph (106) he built the Porticus Minucia on the Campus Martius, later used for grain distributions.

events.title: Lex Coelia tabellaria
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Coelius Caldus extended the secret ballot to trials for perduellio (treason) before the people, completing the series of ballot laws begun in 139. He had been determined to convict Gaius Popillius Laenas for the surrender of his army to the Tigurini.

events.title: Births of Cicero and Pompey
events.summary: Marcus Tullius Cicero was born at Arpinum on 3 January 106 to an equestrian family; Gnaeus Pompeius, son of the Picene grandee Pompeius Strabo, was born on 29 September of the same year, sharing the consular year of Atilius Serranus and Servilius Caepio.

events.title: Marius digs the Fossa Mariana
events.summary: While waiting for the Cimbri and Teutones to return from Spain, Marius had his army dig a canal from the Rhône delta to the sea near Fos, bypassing silted mouths so that supply ships could reach his camp. He later gave the canal and its tolls to Massalia.

events.title: Saturninus' land law for Marius' veterans
events.summary: In his first tribunate Lucius Appuleius Saturninus allotted 100 iugera each in Africa to Marius' Jugurthine veterans, the first settlement of a general's soldiers by tribunician law. The colonists were settled around Thibaris, Uchi Maius and Thuburnica, whose inscriptions later honoured Marius.
events.debate: Dated to 103 by most (Broughton); some argue 100. Evidence for the African settlements is largely epigraphic and later.

events.title: Catulus abandons the Alpine passes
events.summary: The consul Quintus Lutatius Catulus, guarding the Brenner route against the Cimbri, fell back from the Atiso (Adige) when his men panicked; a detachment's fort beyond the river held out and was released by the Cimbri on oath. The Cimbri overran Transpadane Italy that winter.
events.detail: Plutarch, following Sulla's memoirs, says Catulus deliberately led the retreat himself so that the disgrace fell on him rather than the army; the young Sulla was his legate. The episode was later spun by both Catulus and Sulla against Marius.

events.title: Marcus Antonius' command against the pirates
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Antonius, grandfather of the triumvir, received a special command against the pirates of Cilicia, operating from Side and Athens; his fleet was hauled across the Isthmus of Corinth. He triumphed in 100, and Cilicia became a praetorian provincia in the sense of a task.

events.title: Marius' Temple of Honos and Virtus
events.summary: From the spoils of the Cimbri and Teutones, Marius built a temple of Honour and Virtue, probably on the Velia or Capitoline, deliberately kept low so as not to obstruct the augurs' view. Cicero's recall in 57 was voted by the Senate meeting there.

events.title: Murder of Gaius Memmius at the consular elections
events.summary: During the elections for 99, Gaius Memmius, the former tribune who had attacked Jugurtha's patrons, was clubbed to death in the Campus Martius by men linked to Saturninus and Glaucia, who feared he would beat Glaucia to the consulship. The killing turned Marius and the equites against his former allies.

events.title: Birth of Gaius Julius Caesar
events.summary: Gaius Julius Caesar was born on 12 or 13 July, probably in 100, to a patrician family of modest recent success whose aunt Julia had married Marius. The family lived in the Subura.
events.debate: Mommsen preferred 102 to fit the minimum ages of his offices; most now accept 100 and suppose a privilege for patricians or exceptions granted later. Day 12 July (Dio) or 13 July (Macrobius).

events.title: Senate bans human sacrifice
events.summary: In the consulship of Gnaeus Cornelius Lentulus and Publius Licinius Crassus a senatus consultum forbade human sacrifice, a generation after the burial alive of Gauls and Greeks in the Forum Boarium in 114/113. Pliny says the rite had been performed publicly 'even in our own time'.

events.title: Sulla installs Ariobarzanes in Cappadocia
events.summary: After Mithridates and Nicomedes III of Bithynia had both put pretenders on the Cappadocian throne, the Senate let the Cappadocians choose a king; they chose Ariobarzanes I. Sulla, governing Cilicia, installed him with a small force, driving out Gordius and Armenian troops.
events.debate: Date of Sulla's Cilician command disputed: 96 or 92 (Badian argued 96; Keaveney and others 92).

events.title: Lex Varia and the treason trials of 90
events.summary: The tribune Quintus Varius Hybrida set up a special court, staffed by equestrian jurors, to try those who had encouraged the allies to revolt. It struck at the friends of Drusus: Gaius Aurelius Cotta went into exile, Lucius Memmius and others were condemned. Varius himself was condemned under his own law in 89.
events.detail: The aged Scaurus, accused under the law, is said to have answered with a single sentence: 'Varius of Sucro says Scaurus took bribes from the allies; Scaurus denies it; which do you believe?' The court suspended its sittings in the emergency of the war, and in 89 the lex Plautia iudiciaria replaced equestrian juries for it with juries elected by the tribes.

events.title: Vettius Scato defeats Perperna
events.summary: Early in 90 the Roman legate Gaius Perperna lost 4,000 men and most of his weapons to the Marsic-Paelignian commander Publius Vettius Scato. The consul Rutilius Lupus stripped him of his command and transferred his remaining troops to Marius.

battle.significance: One of a string of Italian successes in the first campaigning season.

events.title: Vettius Scato defeats the consul Lucius Caesar
events.summary: The consul Lucius Julius Caesar, commanding the southern front, was defeated by Vettius Scato with the loss of 2,000 men; Venafrum was then betrayed to the Samnite Marius Egnatius, who destroyed two Roman cohorts there.

battle.significance: Opened the Volturnus corridor to the Samnites.

events.title: Siege of Aesernia
events.summary: The Latin colony of Aesernia, held by Lucius Cornelius Scipio and Lucius Acilius (who escaped dressed as slaves), was blockaded by the Samnites through 90 and surrendered from starvation late in the year. It became a rebel stronghold and, in 89/88, the seat of the Italian government after Corfinium.

battle.significance: Gave the insurgents a fortified base in the heart of Samnium.

events.title: Papius Mutilus invades Campania
events.summary: The Samnite commander Gaius Papius Mutilus took Nola by betrayal, executing Roman officers who refused to join him, then captured Stabiae, Minturnae, Salernum and Liternum and enrolled their slaves and prisoners. He besieged Acerrae, the key to Capua.
events.detail: Nola would remain in rebel hands until 80, long after the rest of Italy had surrendered; it was the last town of the Social War to fall. The Campanian campaign showed that the confederates aimed at Rome's resources, not only at defence: Capua's grain and the Campanian ports were vital to the city.

events.title: Siege of Acerrae and Lucius Caesar's victory
events.summary: Lucius Julius Caesar, reinforced by 10,000 Gauls and Numidian horse, held Acerrae against Papius Mutilus and in a sortie killed some 6,000 Samnites, the first real Roman success of the war. The news let Romans in the city put off the military cloak (sagum).

sides.strength: consular army with Gallic and Numidian auxiliaries

battle.significance: Restored morale in Rome; the Numidian cavalry deserted after Mutilus paraded a captured son of Jugurtha, Oxyntas.

events.debate: Appian mentions that Mutilus dressed Oxyntas, a son of Jugurtha held at Venusia, in purple to win over the Numidian troops.

events.title: Poppaedius Silo ambushes Servilius Caepio
events.summary: Quintus Servilius Caepio, sharing command of Rutilius' army with Marius, was lured into an ambush by Quintus Poppaedius Silo, who came over as a pretended deserter with his own sons as hostages and two lumps of gilded lead as treasure. Caepio and most of his force were killed.
events.locName: Marsic territory near the Fucine Lake

battle.significance: Left Marius in sole command of the northern army.

events.title: Marius defeats the Marsi and Marrucini
events.summary: After Rutilius' death Marius, cautious and refusing battle until he chose his ground, defeated the Marsi and Marrucini in a battle in which the Marrucine commander Herius Asinius fell; with Sulla's help some 6,000 rebels were killed. He was nevertheless criticised as slow and resigned the command at year's end.

battle.significance: Stabilised the northern front.

events.title: Pompeius Strabo besieged at Firmum
events.summary: Defeated by the Picene and Marsic commanders Titus Lafrenius, Gaius Vidacilius and Publius Ventidius near Mount Falernus, Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo shut himself up in Firmum. Relieved by Sulpicius, he broke out, killed Lafrenius and drove the rebels back into Asculum.

battle.significance: Opened the siege of Asculum, epicentre of the revolt.

events.title: Etruria and Umbria waver
events.summary: Late in 90 there were risings or threats of revolt among the Umbrians and Etruscans, put down by Aulus Plotius and Lucius Porcius Cato. The danger was a main reason for the lex Julia's offer of citizenship to communities that had stayed loyal or laid down arms.

events.title: Coinage of the Italian insurgents
events.summary: The confederates struck denarii on the Roman standard with Oscan or Latin legends, ITALIA or VITELIU, a helmeted Italia, scenes of eight warriors swearing an oath over a sow, and the Sabellian bull goring the Roman wolf. Issuing generals' names (C. PAAPI, Q. SILO) appear in Oscan.
events.detail: These coins are the confederation's most eloquent surviving documents. The oath scene echoes Roman treaty imagery but with the number of swearers varied; the bull trampling the wolf inverts Rome's founding symbol. Many were overstruck on or imitate Roman denarii, and hoards in central Italy show them circulating with Roman issues. Rare today, they are among the most sought-after Republican coins.

events.title: Death of the consul Lucius Porcius Cato at the Fucine Lake
events.summary: The consul Lucius Porcius Cato, after successes against the Marsi, was killed attacking their camp near the Fucine Lake; Orosius says he was struck down by the son of Marius in the confusion. He was the second consul killed in the war.

battle.significance: Left Pompeius Strabo as sole consul in the field.

events.title: Siege of Pompeii
events.summary: Sulla besieged Pompeii, whose walls still show the impact craters of ballista stones and lead sling bullets; painted Oscan notices (eituns inscriptions) directing defenders to their posts survive on house walls. The town submitted and later received a colony of Sulla's veterans (80).

sides.strength: garrison and Lucius Cluentius' relieving army

battle.significance: Archaeologically the best-documented siege of the war.

events.title: Sulla defeats Cluentius before Nola
events.summary: Attacked while besieging Pompeii by the Samnite Lucius Cluentius, Sulla drove him back to the walls of Nola and, according to Appian, killed 20,000 of his men, including Cluentius. His army awarded him the grass crown (corona graminea), the highest Roman military honour.

battle.significance: Made Sulla's reputation and his consulship for 88.

events.debate: Appian's casualty figure is likely inflated; the grass crown is attested by Pliny, citing Sulla's own memoirs as the likely source.

events.title: Surrender of the Marsi, Vestini and Paeligni
events.summary: During 89 the northern peoples gave up: the Vestini and Marrucini to Servius Sulpicius Galba, the Marsi to Cinna and Caecilius Pius, the Paeligni after the fall of Asculum. The rebel capital moved from Corfinium to Aesernia.

events.title: Lex Papiria reduces the as to half an ounce
events.summary: A lex Papiria, usually dated 91 or 89, reduced the bronze as to the semuncial standard (half an ounce). Bronze was scarcely struck after the 80s until the Augustan reform; the Social War economy ran on denarii, which were minted in record quantities.
events.locName: Mint at the Temple of Juno Moneta
events.debate: Crawford dates the semuncial standard to 91; the law's author is uncertain (perhaps the tribune Gaius Papirius Carbo of 89).

events.title: Nicomedes IV raids Pontus at Roman instigation
events.summary: Pressed by the legate Manius Aquillius and Roman creditors to whom he owed vast sums, Nicomedes IV of Bithynia raided Pontic territory as far as Amastris. Mithridates protested to Rome through his envoy Pelopidas, was rebuffed, and occupied Cappadocia, beginning the First Mithridatic War.
events.detail: Appian gives Pelopidas' speeches at length; they present Mithridates as the injured party and Aquillius as the aggressor, a view many modern historians share. Rome had just ordered Mithridates out of Cappadocia and Bithynia (where he had backed Socrates Chrestus) and he had complied. The Roman commissioners then encouraged a client king to provoke him, apparently believing Pontus too weak to respond and Asia too loyal to waver.

events.title: Sulla destroys Stabiae
events.summary: Sulla, legate in Campania, captured Stabiae on the day before the Kalends of May 89 (29 or 30 April, depending on the calendar reckoning), as Pliny records, and razed it; it survived only as a village of villas, later buried by Vesuvius in AD 79. He went on to besiege Pompeii and Herculaneum.

battle.significance: Began the reconquest of the Bay of Naples.

events.title: Pompeius Strabo enfranchises the Spanish horsemen at Asculum
events.summary: A bronze tablet records that on 17 November 89, in camp before Asculum, Pompeius Strabo granted citizenship 'for valour' to thirty horsemen of the turma Salluitana from the Ebro valley, under the lex Julia. His council (consilium) listed on it includes his son Gnaeus Pompeius (the future Magnus) and the young Lucius Sergius Catilina.
events.detail: The inscription is a snapshot of a Roman army headquarters in the Social War: 59 named officers, many of whom became prominent in the civil wars. It also proves that the lex Julia allowed generals to grant citizenship to individual non-Italians for bravery, the precedent for later grants to provincials.
scholarship: Criniti, L'epigrafe di Asculum di Gn. Pompeo Strabone (1970)

events.title: Death of Poppaedius Silo
events.summary: Silo, who had retaken Bovianum and entered it in triumph, was killed in battle against the praetor Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius in Apulia, ending effective resistance outside Samnium and Lucania.

battle.significance: Effectively ended the confederation as a military power.

events.title: Murder of the consul Quintus Pompeius Rufus
events.summary: Sent to take over Pompeius Strabo's army in Picenum after Sulla's march on Rome, the consul Quintus Pompeius Rufus was killed by Strabo's soldiers while sacrificing, almost certainly with Strabo's connivance. Strabo resumed command.

events.title: Mithridates overruns Roman Asia
events.summary: After routing Nicomedes on the Amnias and the Roman forces at Protopachium, Mithridates swept through Phrygia, Mysia and Ionia almost unopposed. Cities opened their gates and cancelled debts; Lucius Cassius fled to Rhodes, Oppius was surrendered at Laodicea, and Aquillius was handed over at Mytilene. Mithridates made Pergamon and then Ephesus his capital.
events.detail: The speed of the collapse reflects how hated Roman tax-farming and moneylending had become in the province created in 129. Mithridates presented himself as a new Alexander and liberator, remitted taxes for five years, and minted gold staters with an idealised, windswept portrait. The welcome turned sour within two years: the king's demands, executions and arbitrary confiscations drove cities such as Ephesus to revolt in 86.

events.title: Sack of Delos
events.summary: The Pontic general Archelaus (or Menophanes, in Pausanias' version) seized Delos, where Italian merchants had dominated the slave and luxury trade since it became a free port in 166. Some 20,000 people, mainly Italians, were reportedly killed and the island's treasures sent to Athens. A second pirate sack in 69 completed its decline.

battle.significance: Ended Delos as the hub of the Aegean slave trade.

events.debate: The 20,000 figure (Appian) is generally thought exaggerated; the 'Agora of the Italians' shows destruction layers.

events.title: Aristion brings Athens over to Mithridates
events.summary: The Peripatetic philosopher Athenion (called Aristion by most sources), returning from an embassy to Mithridates, persuaded the Athenian assembly to abandon Rome, became general with tyrannical powers, and admitted Archelaus' troops. Athenian silver tetradrachms of 87/86 bear Mithridates' star-and-crescent badge.
events.debate: Whether Athenion and Aristion were one man or two successive leaders is disputed; Posidonius' hostile portrait (preserved by Athenaeus) is our main source.

events.title: Death of Pompeius Strabo
events.summary: Pompeius Strabo, who had played both sides while Cinna and the Senate fought for Rome, died in his camp outside the Colline Gate, according to tradition struck by lightning or of the plague then raging in the camps. The populace dragged his body from its bier.
events.debate: Lightning (Plutarch) or epidemic (Velleius, Orosius); the two may be combined in the tradition.

events.title: Bruttius Sura holds Greece for Rome
events.summary: Quintus Bruttius Sura, legate of the governor of Macedonia, defeated a Pontic fleet off Sciathus and fought Archelaus and Aristion for three days near Chaeronea before Sulla's arrival ordered him back to Macedonia. Plutarch says these fights checked the Pontic advance into Thessaly.

events.title: Sulla requisitions the treasures of Delphi, Olympia and Epidaurus
events.summary: Short of money and cut off from Rome, which was in the hands of his enemies, Sulla seized the dedications of Delphi, Olympia and Epidaurus to pay his army before Athens. When the Delphic envoy reported hearing Apollo's lyre sound from the sanctuary, Sulla replied that it meant the god was pleased to give.
events.detail: He promised to repay the gods and later assigned half the territory of Thebes to the sanctuaries as compensation. The bullion was minted on the spot: Sulla's quaestor Lucius Licinius Lucullus struck large issues of denarii and tetradrachms in Greece, the so-called 'Lucullan' coinage. For later Greeks the episode marked the moment when Roman generals stopped even pretending to respect the panhellenic shrines.

events.title: Suicides of Merula and Catulus
events.summary: When Marius and Cinna took Rome, the flamen Dialis Lucius Cornelius Merula, who had replaced Cinna as consul, opened his veins at the altar of Jupiter, leaving a note that he had first removed his priestly cap. Quintus Lutatius Catulus, victor of Vercellae, shut himself in a freshly plastered room and suffocated himself with charcoal fumes.
events.detail: Merula's death left the flaminate of Jupiter vacant; the teenage Julius Caesar was designated to it in 84/83, a post with taboos (no horse riding, no sight of an army) that would have ended any military career. Sulla's victory voided the appointment. The office stayed empty until 11 BC.

events.title: Mithridates deports the people of Chios
events.summary: Suspecting Chios of Roman sympathies after a Chian ship rammed his flagship off Rhodes, Mithridates demanded 2,000 talents, then declared the payment short, and had his general Zenobius deport the population to the Black Sea in chains. Pontic ships carrying them were intercepted at Heraclea, which returned the Chians home.

events.title: Mithridates massacres the Galatian tetrarchs
events.summary: Fearing the Galatians would join Rome, Mithridates invited sixty Galatian nobles with their families to a banquet at Pergamon and had them killed; one, Deiotarus, escaped and led the Galatian revolt that drove Pontic garrisons out of the country. Deiotarus became Rome's most loyal client in Anatolia.

events.title: The Asian cities turn against Mithridates
events.summary: After Chaeronea, Ephesus rose against Mithridates' governor Zenobius and decreed war on the king; Tralles, Hypaepa, Metropolis, Sardis and Colophon followed. Mithridates answered with a counter-programme of freeing slaves, cancelling debts and granting citizenship to resident aliens in cities that stayed loyal. The Ephesian decree survives on stone.

sources.r: Ephesian decree of war against Mithridates

events.title: Lucullus' naval victory off Tenedos
events.summary: Sulla's quaestor Lucius Licinius Lucullus, who had spent the winter collecting ships from Cyprus, Phoenicia, Rhodes and Pamphylia, defeated a Pontic fleet under Neoptolemus near Lectum and Tenedos. He then refused Fimbria's request to blockade Mithridates at Pitane, letting the king escape by sea to Mytilene.

battle.significance: Gave Sulla command of the Aegean for the crossing to Asia.

events.debate: Plutarch's claim that Lucullus let Mithridates escape out of loyalty to Sulla over Fimbria is often repeated; it may be a later rationalisation.

events.title: Fimbria sacks Ilium
events.summary: Gaius Flavius Fimbria, having taken over Flaccus' army, besieged Ilium, which wished to surrender to Sulla, took it after eleven days and destroyed it, boasting that he had done in eleven days what Agamemnon needed ten years for. A citizen replied that the Trojans then had had Hector.

battle.significance: A Roman army destroying the mother city of Rome's own legend; Sulla later rebuilt and freed it.

events.title: Suicide of Fimbria
events.summary: Sulla, after the peace of Dardanus, marched against Fimbria near Thyatira; Fimbria's men deserted to him, and Fimbria, after a failed attempt to have Sulla assassinated, killed himself in the temple of Asclepius at Pergamon. His two legions, the Valeriani, were left in Asia and served Lucullus for years.

events.title: The Rhetorica ad Herennium
events.summary: The earliest complete Latin handbook of rhetoric, dedicated to one Gaius Herennius, was written in the 80s by an author with popularis sympathies; its examples come from the Social War and the 90s. Long attributed to Cicero, it was the standard medieval rhetorical textbook and contains the classic account of the 'memory palace'.
events.debate: Author unknown (Cornificius has been proposed); date c. 86-82 inferred from internal references.

events.title: Sulla's imperatorial gold
events.summary: Sulla's eastern mint struck the first substantial Roman gold coinage since the Second Punic War: aurei and denarii naming him IMPER ITERVM with trophies, jug and lituus, and his quaestor Manlius Torquatus' issue showing Sulla in a triumphal quadriga crowned by Victory. They paid the army that was about to invade Italy.
events.detail: This is the first time a Roman general put his own power, rather than his family's history, at the centre of coinage. The two trophies probably allude to Chaeronea and Orchomenus. The aureus became, with Caesar and the triumvirs, the instrument of army pay in the civil wars, and gold issues became normal only after 49.

events.title: New citizens distributed through all thirty-five tribes
events.summary: The Cinnan regime gave effect to Sulpicius' programme: a decree of the Senate distributed the enfranchised Italians and freedmen among all thirty-five tribes rather than confining them to a few. The censors of 86 had registered only 463,000 citizens, showing how incomplete enrolment of the new citizens still was.
events.debate: The census figure of 86 (463,000) against 910,000 in 70 shows the real enfranchisement of Italy happened over a generation; why the 86 registration was so low (war, hostility of censors, refusal to register) is debated.

events.title: Murena raids Pontus: the Second Mithridatic War begins
events.summary: Lucius Licinius Murena, left by Sulla in Asia with Fimbria's legions, claimed Mithridates was arming and raided Pontic Cappadocia, plundering the rich temple-town of Comana. The Senate's envoy Calidius ordered him to stop, but in 82 he invaded again and was defeated on the Halys.

events.title: The army of the consul Scipio goes over to Sulla near Teanum
events.summary: Encamped near Teanum Sidicinum, the consul Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus negotiated with Sulla; during a truce Sulla's soldiers fraternised with Scipio's and the whole consular army defected. Scipio, captured in his tent with his son, was released. Carbo said he had to fight a fox and a lion in Sulla, and the fox gave more trouble.
events.detail: Sertorius, serving with Scipio, had warned against the talks; the betrayal convinced him that the Marian cause in Italy was lost and he left for Spain. The episode, like the earlier defeat of Norbanus at Mount Tifata, showed that many Roman soldiers would not fight Sulla's veterans.

events.title: Pompey raises a private army in Picenum
events.summary: Gnaeus Pompeius, aged twenty-three and holding no office, raised three legions from his father's clients in Picenum, set up his tribunal at Auximum, drove out the Carbonian recruiting officers and defeated three enemy commanders before joining Sulla, who saluted him as imperator.
events.detail: The episode is the clearest example of the 'private army' of the late Republic: soldiers loyal to a family rather than to the state. Velleius and Plutarch tell it as heroic; Sallust and others later remembered the adulescentulus carnifex, the teenage butcher. Crassus and Metellus Pius also brought forces to Sulla at this time.

events.title: Sertorius leaves for Spain
events.summary: Despairing of the Marian leadership, Quintus Sertorius took up his province of Hither Spain late in 83, raising troops and paying the passes of the Pyrenean tribes for passage. Expelled in 81 by Gaius Annius, he fled to Mauretania before the Lusitanians called him back in 80.

events.title: Battles around Clusium
events.summary: In the northern theatre Sulla fought Carbo near Clusium in a day-long indecisive battle, while Pompey and Crassus defeated Carbo's lieutenant Carrinas near Spoletium. Carbo, losing hope after Faventia and the defection of his lieutenants, fled to Africa.

battle.significance: Pinned Carbo's main army while Praeneste was besieged.

events.title: Damasippus' massacre of senators
events.summary: On orders sent by the besieged younger Marius, the praetor Lucius Junius Brutus Damasippus summoned the Senate and had leading suspected Sullan sympathisers killed in the Curia Hostilia, including the pontifex maximus Quintus Mucius Scaevola, cut down at the entrance to the temple of Vesta, and the ex-praetor Papirius Carbo Arvina.
events.detail: The murder of Scaevola, the greatest jurist of the age and a man who had tried to stay neutral, horrified contemporaries; Cicero cites it repeatedly. It gave Sulla moral cover for the proscriptions, and Damasippus himself was killed after the Colline Gate.

events.title: Caesar refuses to divorce Cinna's daughter
events.summary: Ordered by Sulla to divorce Cornelia, Cinna's daughter, the eighteen-year-old Julius Caesar refused, lost his priesthood and his wife's dowry, and went into hiding in Sabine country, bribing his way past patrols while sick with fever. Sulla relented at the pleas of the Vestals and Caesar's relatives, warning that there were many Mariuses in him.
events.debate: Sulla's prophetic remark is surely a later embellishment.

events.title: Cicero's first surviving speech: Pro Quinctio
events.summary: Cicero, aged twenty-five, defended Publius Quinctius in a civil suit over a Gallic partnership against Sextus Naevius, a crier backed by the great orator Hortensius and by powerful Sullan connections. The speech is the earliest surviving Ciceronian oration.

events.title: Pompey's African triumph
events.summary: Pompey, still an eques who had held no magistracy, extorted from Sulla a triumph for his African victories over Domitius Ahenobarbus and King Iarbas, celebrated on 12 March. His chariot, drawn by elephants, could not pass through the triumphal gate and he had to switch to horses.
events.debate: Year disputed: 81 (Badian, Seager), 80, or 79 (Granius Licinianus' evidence read differently). Sulla reportedly gave way after Pompey told him more men worship the rising than the setting sun.

events.title: Sertorius defeats Cotta off Mellaria
events.summary: Returning from Mauretania with Lusitanian support, Sertorius beat Sulla's legate Aurelius Cotta in a sea battle in the Strait near Mellaria, then crossed into Spain and defeated the governor Fufidius on the Baetis.

battle.significance: Let Sertorius establish himself in Lusitania.

events.title: Murder of Ptolemy XI and accession of Ptolemy XII
events.summary: Ptolemy XI Alexander II, installed by Sulla, murdered his co-ruler and stepmother Berenice III after nineteen days and was lynched by the Alexandrians. They chose an illegitimate son of Ptolemy IX, Ptolemy XII 'Neos Dionysos', nicknamed Auletes (the flute-player). Rumour said Alexander II, or his predecessor Alexander I, had bequeathed Egypt to Rome.
events.detail: The supposed will hung over Auletes' whole reign. Rome never formally acted on it, but it gave politicians such as Crassus (65) and Rullus (63) a pretext for proposing annexation, and it is the reason Auletes spent a fortune buying recognition as 'friend and ally of the Roman people' (59).
events.debate: Whether the will existed and which Alexander made it was uncertain even to Cicero.

events.title: Cicero studies in Athens and Rhodes
events.summary: Partly for his health and partly, Plutarch suggests, to avoid Sulla after the Roscius case, Cicero spent two years in Athens, Asia and Rhodes, hearing Antiochus of Ascalon, the Epicurean Zeno, and the rhetorician Apollonius Molon, who taught him to restrain his strained, full-voiced delivery. Posidonius was also among his teachers.
events.detail: Cicero's own account in the Brutus tells how he returned 'not just better trained but almost transformed'. In Athens he befriended Titus Pomponius, henceforth Atticus. The trip was the formative moment of the Roman philosophical education; Caesar would go to Molon at Rhodes a few years later.

events.title: Sertorius relieves Lacobriga
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius besieged the Lusitanian town of Lacobriga, expecting it to fall within days for lack of water; Sertorius smuggled in 2,000 skins of water, evacuated non-combatants and ambushed Metellus' foraging legion, forcing him to withdraw.

battle.significance: Typical of Sertorius' guerrilla success against Metellus' heavy columns.

events.title: Rising at Faesulae
events.summary: Dispossessed farmers at Faesulae in Etruria attacked the Sullan veterans settled on their land and killed several. The Senate sent both consuls, Lepidus and Catulus, to deal with it; Lepidus took the side of the rebels, the prelude to his revolt.

events.title: Servilius Vatia's war in Cilicia and Isauria
events.summary: Publius Servilius Vatia, proconsul of Cilicia, won a sea battle against the pirates, took the strongholds of the pirate chief Zenicetes on Mount Olympus in Lycia, and was the first Roman to lead an army over the Taurus, capturing Isaura by diverting its water supply. He earned the cognomen Isauricus.

events.title: Catulus builds the Tabularium
events.summary: Quintus Lutatius Catulus, as consul of 78, built a massive record office on the slope of the Capitol above the Forum, whose arcaded façade of Gabine stone and tufa still forms the base of the Palazzo Senatorio. The identification with the state archive rests on an inscription naming Catulus' substructio et tabularium.
events.debate: Whether the building was the tabularium of the state or a substructure for Capitoline temples has been questioned (Tucci, 2005).

events.title: Pompey besieges Brutus at Mutina
events.summary: Marching against the Lepidan forces in Cisalpine Gaul, Pompey besieged Marcus Junius Brutus, father of the tyrannicide, in Mutina. Brutus surrendered and was killed the next day at Regium Lepidi by Pompey's agent Geminius, an act later held against Pompey.

battle.significance: Ended the Lepidan threat in the north.

events.title: Pompey opens a new road over the Alps
events.summary: On his way to Spain Pompey cut a new route through the Cottian Alps, probably over the Mont Genèvre, fighting the mountain tribes. In his letter of 75 he boasted that he had opened a road different from Hannibal's and more convenient for Rome. He wintered among the Vocontii and Gallic tribes he later settled.

events.title: Sertorius' school for the children of Spanish nobles
events.summary: Sertorius gathered the sons of the leading Spanish families at Osca (Huesca), dressed them in the toga praetexta, and had them taught Greek and Latin by Roman teachers. It was a civilising gesture and a means of holding hostages; Perperna's faction later used it as a grievance.

events.title: Pompey destroys Herennius and Perperna at Valentia
events.summary: Early in 75 Pompey defeated Sertorius' lieutenants Gaius Herennius and Marcus Perperna outside Valentia, killing 10,000 and Herennius, and sacked the city. Archaeologists have found the skeletons of executed and mutilated men in a destruction layer dated to this event.

battle.significance: Opened the east coast to Pompey.

scholarship: Ribera i Lacomba and Calvo Galvez, 'La primera evidencia arqueológica de la destrucción de Valentia por Pompeyo', JRA 8 (1995)

events.title: Pompey's letter to the Senate
events.summary: Short of pay and grain after the campaigns of 75, Pompey wrote to the Senate threatening that unless supplies arrived his army, and with it the Spanish war, would cross into Italy. The consul Lucius Lucullus, eager to keep Pompey in Spain and away from the Mithridatic command, ensured money was sent.
events.debate: The text in Sallust's Histories is a Sallustian composition, not a verbatim letter.

events.title: Cicero quaestor at Lilybaeum
events.summary: As quaestor in western Sicily, Cicero shipped grain to Rome during a shortage and won the Sicilians' trust; on his tour he rediscovered Archimedes' overgrown tomb near Syracuse by its sphere and cylinder. Returning, he found that Rome had barely noticed his absence, a lesson he says he never forgot.

events.title: Antonius' command against the pirates and defeat by Crete
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Antonius, father of the triumvir, received an unlimited command (imperium infinitum) over the coasts against the pirates. After requisitioning heavily in Sicily and Greece, he attacked Crete and was defeated at sea near Cydonia; his captured men were hung from the ships' rigging. He died soon after, mocked with the cognomen Creticus.
events.detail: The command was the precedent for Pompey's lex Gabinia, but its failure was spectacular. Rome's retaliation came with Quintus Caecilius Metellus' conquest of Crete (69-67).

events.title: Cyrene organised as a province
events.summary: Twenty-two years after Ptolemy Apion's bequest, the Senate sent the quaestor Publius Cornelius Lentulus Marcellinus to administer Cyrenaica as a province, largely to exploit the royal lands and secure grain during the shortage of the 70s.

events.title: The iudicium Iunianum: bribed jurors in the Oppianicus case
events.summary: A senatorial jury under Gaius Junius condemned Statius Albius Oppianicus for attempting to poison his stepson Aulus Cluentius; it emerged that both sides had bribed jurors, and that one juror, Staienus, had pocketed the money. The scandal became the standing proof that senatorial juries could be bought, fuel for the jury reform of 70.
